newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA COSATU SEES DISPUTE SETTLED IN PARLIAMENT.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA COSATU SEES DISPUTE SETTLED IN PARLIAMENT.

text.p: South Africa's biggest labour body the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) said on Friday that its dispute with government and management on a new labour law would be settled in parliament.
The proposed Basic Conditions of Employment Bill is set to go for discussion to the statutory National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) in the next few weeks.
Cosatu said the Nedlac talks held little hope of reaching a settlement and the process would benefit if the talks were kept as short as possible.
"We do not believe that further negotiations will produce anything in Nedlac at this point in time," Cosatu general secretary Sam Shilowa told a news conference.
Shilowa said Cosatu would contact the African National Congress and South African Communist Party and seek to ammend the labour law as it passed through parliament.
Earlier Cosatu said it planned to go ahead with a half day of national action on May 12 with marches and protests converging on employer's associations around the country.
But the half day strike is a step back from the full 24 hour stoppage originally announced in February.
Shilowa said since Cosatu had threatened the action some progress on adjusting the proposed laws had been made.
"The situation as it was in February, to the situation now is different," he said.

Labour Minister Tito Mboweni released the bill on Thursday, and in line with policy plans previously outlined, the bill retained proposals to reduce weekly working hours to 45 from 46 hours for all workers, including mine, farm and shift workers.

Shilowa welcomed the move saying it would improve the lot of two million South African workers, but added Costau's original aim of a 40 hour maximum should be included in the law as should a future objective with details of when it would be achieved.

Other proposals include an increase in annual paid leave from two to three weeks a year and maternity leave from three months to four months as well as raising overtime from time and a third to time an half.
Shilowa welcomed these developments, but said Cosatu reiterated its demands for a six month period of maternity leave with four months being paid.
Shilowa also criticised elements in the bill which allow for employers and workers to agree local variations in working standards.
"We remain opposed to the principal of variation contained in the bill...we remain in dispute on this issue," he said.
The argument over the bill has placed South African labour and business in clear opposition to each other.
South African organised business says it fears the bill, approved by the cabinet this week, would increase labour costs.

"These increased benefits represent additional costs to the individual business enterprise and will add to overall unit labour costs," South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) president Philip Krawitz said in a statement.
But the chamber said it welcomed the absence of a statutory imposed goal of a 40-hour work week.
